summary:
Farmers Compass is a free web app that lets a farmer test crop rotations on their own field before planting them.

The farmer picks their field on a map and chooses what matters most: soil health, water use, yield or risk. The app tries 419 possible rotations of corn, alfalfa, grass, barley and soybean. It runs each one through 1,000 possible 20-year futures, built from 30 years of real NASA weather for that exact spot. It then shows the top 10 rotations and how often each one beats the farmer’s current plan.

NASA data drives every step:

Daymet and POWER provide the weather and soil wetness used in the ranking.
NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 lets farmers test their plan under the 2050 climate.
MODIS field greenness and the GEOS 10-day forecast add context.

This matters because farmers commit to rotations years ahead without knowing the weather. A bad choice can cost yield, water and soil health for years, and most small farms can’t afford an agronomist. Farmers Compass turns NASA Earth data into a clear, field-specific answer anyone can use.
details:
What it does

Farmers Compass is a web app that recommends crop rotations for a farmer’s own field. It works in three steps:

  1. Pick your field. The farmer clicks their field on a map and chooses the soil type.
  2. Set your goals. Four sliders set how much the farmer cares about soil health, water use, yield and risk (yield in a bad year).
  3. See the results. The app shows the top 10 rotations and how often each one beats the farmer’s current rotation.

How it works

  • Weather data: it pulls 30 years of real daily weather (1995 to 2024) for that exact spot from NASA Daymet and NASA POWER.
    • Each rotation is 4 to 6 years long.
    • They follow common farming rules: an annual crop at most 2 years in a row, and a perennial at least 3.
    • Each rotation is tested with and without a cover crop.
  • Score: each rotation gets a score weighted by the four sliders. The “win rate” is how often it beats the farmer’s current plan across the 1,000 futures.
  • 2050 option: NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections let farmers test their plan under the 2050 climate.
  • Extra context: MODIS field greenness and the GEOS 10-day forecast are shown on the page.

Benefits

  • Advice for the farmer’s exact field, not a regional average.
  • It shows risk, not just the average: how often a rotation wins, and how it does in bad years.
  • It’s free and runs in a browser, with no agronomist needed.
  • It’s transparent: the coefficients come from published sources (FAO-56, Statistics Canada, OMAFRA, Perennia, and peer-reviewed soil carbon studies).

Intended impact

The app helps small and mid-size farms choose rotations that protect soil and water without guessing. Example (Annapolis Valley, loam soil, a farmer who cares most about soil health): the top pick beats the farmer’s current rotation in all 1,000 futures. Under the 2050 climate, it gives much healthier soil and uses 10% less water, but produces 17% less feed. The farmer sees that trade-off before committing to it.

Tools and technology

  • Backend: Python and FastAPI (6 routes)
  • Simulator: NumPy, or CuPy when a GPU is available, so all 1,000 futures run at once
  • Frontend: a single HTML page with MapLibre for the map
  • Data: NASA Daymet, POWER, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, MODIS and GEOS, cached on disk so the app stays fast
  • Hardware: standard laptops, with an optional GPU
  • Code: https://github.com/shauryaslab/FarmersCompass

What makes it creative

Most tools give a single yield forecast. Farmers Compass instead asks, “How often does this plan beat yours?”, using futures built from real NASA weather. It turns climate data into a simple, farmer-facing decision and shows the trade-offs between goals.

Factors we considered

  • Simplicity: no jargon, four sliders, and a clear top 10.
  • Honesty about limits: the model doesn’t yet cover heat and frost damage, detailed soil, actual harvest records, droughts several years in a row, or prices and crop quality. Some coefficients are borrowed from nearby regions. We list these in the app and in our pitch.
  • Local fit: crops, soils and numbers were chosen for Nova Scotia and Atlantic Canada.
  • Speed: cached data and GPU support give results in seconds.
  • Access: free, browser-based and mobile-friendly.
